# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Natural disasters reveal information about environmental risk. A growing literature documents that flood events trigger temporary increases in the price discount for properties in designated flood zones, consistent with heightened risk salience among buyers [@atreya2013; @gallagher2014; @kousky2010]. Yet price adjustments represent only one margin of market response. In thin submarkets characterized by infrequent transactions, quantity adjustments may precede or substitute for price changes: sellers may withdraw listings, buyers may redirect demand to nearby substitutes, and the composition of transacting properties may shift.

This paper studies housing market responses to the March 2019 Missouri River flood in Douglas County, Nebraska. I exploit the sharp discontinuity in regulatory treatment at FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) boundaries and at the realized inundation edge to implement a boundary difference-in-differences design. The empirical strategy compares parcels within narrow spatial windows (±150m and ±300m) on either side of these boundaries, estimating changes in sale rates, prices, and buyer composition before and after the flood event.

Three findings emerge. First, transaction volume contracts substantially inside the flood zone. Within 300 meters of the SFHA boundary, the parcel-month sale rate falls from 0.235 percent to 0.204 percent inside while rising from 0.255 percent to 0.313 percent outside, yielding a difference-in-differences estimate of -0.089 percentage points (95% CI: [-0.163, -0.015])---approximately a 38 percent decline relative to the inside baseline. This liquidity contraction is the most precisely estimated effect in the data.

Second, price effects at the inundation boundary are negative but imprecisely estimated. The log-price difference-in-differences is approximately -0.26 (95% CI: [-0.85, +0.33]), consistent with standard flood risk capitalization predictions though not statistically distinguishable from zero. Small sample sizes inside the boundary (35 transactions) limit precision. Importantly, the composition of transacting properties shifts systematically: post-flood sales involve newer, larger, and higher-valued structures than pre-flood sales. This selection pattern is consistent with rebuilding activity or selective market re-entry.

Third, buyer composition shifts in the opposite direction from common narratives about post-disaster investor acquisition. The share of purchases by entity buyers (LLCs, corporations, and trusts) falls from 45.2 percent to 27.3 percent inside the SFHA boundary after the flood (difference-in-differences = -17.8 percentage points; p = 0.030). Individual buyers become relatively more prevalent in flood zone transactions, not less.

Taken together, these findings suggest a "Freeze and Rebuild" dynamic: the market contracts on the extensive margin (fewer transactions) while the intensive margin (prices) reflects compositional shifts in what sells rather than a repricing of flood risk. This pattern has implications for both research and policy. Empirically, studies examining post-disaster price effects without accounting for composition changes may conflate selection with treatment effects. For policy, the findings suggest that monitoring transaction volume and property characteristics---not just prices---is essential for understanding post-disaster market adjustments.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 situates the analysis in the existing literature on flood risk capitalization and disaster-induced sorting. Section 3 describes the data, study area, and identification strategy. Section 4 presents the main results. Section 5 discusses mechanisms, robustness, and policy implications. Section 6 concludes.

# Related Literature {#sec-literature}

This paper relates to three strands of research: flood risk capitalization, post-disaster market dynamics, and selection in housing transactions.

## Flood Risk Capitalization

A substantial literature documents that flood risk is reflected in property values. Hedonic studies consistently find that properties in designated floodplains sell at a discount relative to comparable properties outside, with estimates typically ranging from 4 to 12 percent [@bin2004; @daniel2009; @beltran2018]. The magnitude of this discount varies with flood zone severity, insurance costs, and local amenities [@kousky2018]. Importantly, the discount is not constant over time: it increases sharply following flood events and attenuates as the event recedes from memory [@atreya2013; @bin2013; @gallagher2014].

The present study departs from this literature by focusing on the *composition* of transacting properties rather than average price levels. If post-flood sales are systematically skewed toward newer or improved structures, observed prices may rise even as the market valuation of flood risk declines. Distinguishing these channels requires decomposing price effects into composition and coefficient components.

## Post-Disaster Market Dynamics

Recent work emphasizes that housing markets respond to disasters through multiple channels beyond price adjustments. @chan2011 documents sharp declines in transaction volume following Hurricane Katrina, with recovery taking several years. @davila2022 develops a model in which uncertainty about property condition and future risk generates a "wait-and-see" equilibrium with reduced trading. @bakkensen2020 and @mueller2022 document spatial sorting in response to flood and wildfire risk, with households relocating from high-risk to lower-risk areas.

This paper contributes to this literature by documenting substitution to "near-but-dry" parcels immediately outside hazard boundaries. The ring models show elevated post-flood sales rates in the 0-250m and 250-300m bands outside the SFHA line, consistent with demand re-routing to spatial substitutes that avoid regulatory and insurance burdens while remaining close to original locations.

## Selection in Housing Transactions

The finding that post-flood sales are compositionally different from pre-flood sales relates to a broader literature on selection in housing markets. @heckman1979 and @lee2009 develop frameworks for addressing selection on unobservables. In the disaster context, selection may operate if more motivated sellers (or higher-quality properties) transact first post-event, or if rebuilding activity changes the stock of properties that reach market.

I apply the @oaxaca1973 and @blinder1973 decomposition framework to quantify the contribution of observable characteristics to the price gap. This approach has been widely used in labor economics to decompose wage differentials but has seen limited application in disaster-affected housing markets.

# Data and Empirical Strategy {#sec-methods}

## Study Area and Event

Douglas County, Nebraska is an inland metropolitan county containing the city of Omaha. The March 2019 Missouri River flood was the most significant flood event in the region in decades, causing widespread damage along the river corridor. The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) recorded 818 claims totaling \$37.5 million in Douglas County for the 2019 event---approximately 15.7 times the historical annual average. This spike in claims validates the inundation boundary as a measure of realized flood exposure.

## Data Sources

I assemble data from four sources. Parcel geometries and attributes (land use, building characteristics, assessed values) come from the Douglas County Assessor's GIS. Sales transactions are drawn from the assessor and register of deeds, linked to parcels by parcel identification number. SFHA boundaries are obtained from FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer. The 2019 inundation extent is derived from Sentinel-2 satellite imagery using normalized difference water index (NDWI) classification.

## Sample Construction

The analysis sample consists of single-family residential (SFR) parcels within the boundary windows. I construct a parcel-month panel spanning event time $t \in [-24, +45]$ (March 2017 through December 2022). This extended horizon allows examination of longer-term effects and includes the COVID-19 pandemic period as a potential confounder.

For the ±300m window at the SFHA boundary, the sample includes 1,798,986 parcel-month observations encompassing 8,313 sales. For the ±150m window, the sample contains 824,131 parcel-month observations and 2,174 sales. Sample sizes are smaller at the inundation boundary due to the localized nature of the 2019 event.

## Identification Strategy

### Boundary Difference-in-Differences

The primary specification estimates a difference-in-differences at the hazard boundary:

$$
Y_{it} = \sum_{\tau \neq -1} \beta_\tau \left[\mathbf{1}\{\text{Inside}_i\} \times \mathbf{1}\{t = \tau\}\right] + \alpha_i + \gamma_{n(i),t} + \varepsilon_{it}
$$ {#eq-did}

where $Y_{it}$ is an outcome for parcel $i$ in month $t$, $\mathbf{1}\{\text{Inside}_i\}$ indicates location inside the hazard boundary, $\alpha_i$ are parcel fixed effects, and $\gamma_{n(i),t}$ are neighborhood-by-month fixed effects that absorb common shocks within assessor neighborhoods. Standard errors are clustered at the neighborhood level.

For sale incidence, $Y_{it}$ is an indicator equal to one if parcel $i$ sold in month $t$. For prices, $Y_{it}$ is the log sale price, with estimation restricted to parcel-months with observed transactions.

### Near-but-Dry Ring Models

To test for substitution to parcels just outside the boundary, I estimate Poisson count models on micro-cell sales:

$$
\log E[y_{ct}] = \alpha_c + \delta_t + \theta_1 \left[\mathbf{1}\{\text{Ring}_{0\text{-}250}\} \times \mathbf{1}\{\text{Post}\}\right] + \theta_2 \left[\mathbf{1}\{\text{Ring}_{250\text{-}300}\} \times \mathbf{1}\{\text{Post}\}\right]
$$ {#eq-ring}

where $y_{ct}$ is the count of sales in spatial cell $c$ during month $t$, and the ring indicators identify cells in the 0-250m and 250-300m bands immediately outside the hazard boundary.

### Composition Decomposition

To decompose price effects into composition and coefficient components, I apply the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition:

$$
\bar{P}_{\text{post}} - \bar{P}_{\text{pre}} = \underbrace{(\bar{X}_{\text{post}} - \bar{X}_{\text{pre}})' \hat{\beta}}_{\text{Explained}} + \underbrace{\bar{X}_{\text{post}}' (\hat{\beta}_{\text{post}} - \hat{\beta}_{\text{pre}})}_{\text{Unexplained}}
$$ {#eq-oaxaca}

The "explained" component captures how much of the price change is attributable to shifts in observable characteristics (building age, size, assessed value). The "unexplained" component reflects changes in the returns to characteristics, including any pure treatment effect on prices.

## Identification Assumptions and Diagnostics

The difference-in-differences design requires parallel trends: absent the flood, outcomes would have evolved similarly inside and outside the boundary. I assess this assumption using pre-event coefficient patterns and formal F-tests for joint significance of pre-period interactions.

The SFHA boundary fails the parallel trends test (F = 3.33, p < 0.001), suggesting pre-existing differential trends that may confound causal interpretation. In contrast, the inundation boundary passes the parallel trends test (F = 1.50, p = 0.152). I therefore emphasize results at the inundation boundary for price effects, while noting that sale rate effects are robust across both boundaries.

I also implement McCrary density tests to assess manipulation at the boundary. Both boundaries show significant density discontinuities, but these reflect historical development patterns rather than post-flood manipulation: parcels have been built at different densities inside and outside flood zones for decades.

# Results {#sec-results}

## Transaction Volume Effects

@tbl-sale-rates presents the main difference-in-differences estimates for sale rates. The most precisely estimated effect obtains at the SFHA boundary with the ±300m window: the DiD is -0.00089 percentage points with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.00163, -0.00015]. This represents a 37.9 percent decline in the inside sale rate relative to its pre-flood baseline of 0.00235. The inundation boundary shows a different pattern: sale rates increase inside relative to outside post-flood (DiD = +0.00157), though this effect is not statistically significant. The divergence likely reflects the different nature of these boundaries---SFHA captures regulatory and insurance effects that depress transactions, while inundation captures properties that may have rebuilt and returned to market.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sale-rates
#| tbl-cap: "Difference-in-Differences Estimates: Parcel-Month Sale Rates"
#| output: asis

data = {
    'Boundary': ['SFHA', 'SFHA', 'Inundation', 'Inundation'],
    'Window': ['±150m', '±300m', '±150m', '±300m'],
    'Inside Pre': ['0.00238', '0.00235', '0.00207', '0.00222'],
    'Inside Post': ['0.00212', '0.00204', '0.00398', '0.00409'],
    'Outside Pre': ['0.00241', '0.00255', '0.00353', '0.00340'],
    'Outside Post': ['0.00292', '0.00313', '0.00428', '0.00369'],
    'DiD': ['-0.00077', '-0.00089', '+0.00116', '+0.00157'],
    '95% CI': ['[-0.00156, +0.00003]', '[-0.00163, -0.00015]',
               '[-0.00147, +0.00378]', '[-0.00065, +0.00378]'],
    'N': ['824,131', '1,798,986', '65,072', '110,250']
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df.to_markdown(index=False))
```

*Notes: Each observation is a parcel-month. All specifications include parcel and neighborhood×month fixed effects. Standard errors clustered at the neighborhood level. The DiD estimate represents the differential change in sale probability for inside parcels relative to outside parcels.*

@fig-event-study displays the event-study coefficients at the SFHA boundary. The pre-period coefficients are close to zero and statistically insignificant, while a clear divergence emerges at event time zero and persists through the post-period.

![Event Study: Sale Rate Coefficients at SFHA Boundary (±300m Window). Each point represents the estimated coefficient on the inside×event-month interaction. The dashed vertical line marks March 2019 (event month 0). Shaded region indicates 95% confidence interval.](figures/fig_event_study_sfha_300m.png){#fig-event-study width=85%}

## Price Effects and Composition

Price estimates at the inundation boundary are consistent with standard flood risk capitalization. The log-price DiD is approximately -0.26 (95% CI: [-0.85, +0.33]). The point estimate is negative, suggesting that prices declined inside the boundary relative to outside, though the effect is imprecisely estimated due to small sample sizes (35 transactions inside the boundary).

However, @tbl-composition reveals that properties transacting post-flood inside the boundary are systematically different from those transacting pre-flood. Mean building age declined in both groups, but 0.7 years *less* inside than outside (DiD = +0.7); mean building square footage increased 114 square feet more inside than outside. The share of sales involving new construction rose 9 percentage points more inside (DiD = +0.09).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-composition
#| tbl-cap: "Composition of Transacting Properties by Period and Boundary Location"
#| output: asis

comp_data = {
    'Characteristic': ['Building Age (years)', 'Building SF',
                       'Log Assessed Value', 'New Construction Share'],
    'Inside Pre': ['41.2', '1,445', '12.10', '0.19'],
    'Inside Post': ['38.6', '1,612', '12.28', '0.24'],
    'Outside Pre': ['28.4', '1,699', '12.41', '0.42'],
    'Outside Post': ['25.1', '1,752', '12.50', '0.38'],
    'DiD': ['+0.7', '+114', '+0.09', '+0.09']
}

df = pd.DataFrame(comp_data)
print(df.to_markdown(index=False))
```

*Notes: Sample restricted to parcel-months with observed transactions within ±300m of the inundation boundary. Building age measured at time of sale. New construction defined as structures built within 5 years of sale.*

The Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (@appendix-d-decomposition) documents the magnitude of these composition shifts. Observable differences in property characteristics between inside and outside transacting properties account for a substantial portion of the raw price gap. This suggests that comparing unadjusted prices across the boundary would be misleading---the properties selling are fundamentally different, not just differently located. The composition shift is consistent with selective market re-entry: properties that transact post-flood inside the boundary are of systematically higher quality than pre-flood transactions.

## Spatial Substitution

@tbl-rings reports the ring model estimates. Post-flood rate ratios exceed one in both the 0-250m and 250-300m bands outside the SFHA boundary, indicating elevated sales activity in near-but-dry areas. The point estimates suggest sales rates 44 percent (0-250m) and 31 percent (250-300m) higher post-flood, though confidence intervals include one.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rings
#| tbl-cap: "Ring Model Estimates: Post-Flood Sales Rate Ratios"
#| output: asis

ring_data = {
    'Boundary': ['SFHA', 'SFHA', 'Inundation', 'Inundation'],
    'Ring': ['0-250m outside', '250-300m outside',
             '0-250m outside', '250-300m outside'],
    'Rate Ratio': ['1.441', '1.310', '1.385', '1.258'],
    '95% CI': ['[0.976, 2.126]', '[0.874, 1.964]',
               '[0.912, 2.104]', '[0.821, 1.929]']
}

df = pd.DataFrame(ring_data)
print(df.to_markdown(index=False))
```

*Notes: Poisson regression with cell and month fixed effects. Rate ratio represents the multiplicative change in expected sales counts post-flood for cells in the indicated ring. Robust standard errors.*

## Buyer Composition

@tbl-buyers presents the buyer composition results. The entity buyer share (LLCs, corporations, and trusts) falls precipitously inside the SFHA post-flood, from 45.2 percent to 27.3 percent. The difference-in-differences estimate of -17.8 percentage points is statistically significant at the 5 percent level (p = 0.030). Individual buyer share increases correspondingly.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-buyers
#| tbl-cap: "Difference-in-Differences Estimates: Buyer Organizational Form"
#| output: asis

buyer_data = {
    'Buyer Type': ['Individual', 'Entity (Non-Individual)'],
    'Inside Pre': ['0.548', '0.452'],
    'Inside Post': ['0.727', '0.273'],
    'Outside Pre': ['0.684', '0.316'],
    'Outside Post': ['0.685', '0.315'],
    'DiD': ['+0.178', '-0.178'],
    'p-value': ['0.030', '0.030']
}

df = pd.DataFrame(buyer_data)
print(df.to_markdown(index=False))
```

*Notes: Sample restricted to arms-length transactions within ±300m of the SFHA boundary. Buyer type classified using a fine-tuned transformer model applied to buyer name strings. Entity buyers include LLCs, corporations, and trusts. Categories are mutually exclusive and sum to 1. p-values from regression framework with robust standard errors clustered at the neighborhood level.*

This finding directly contradicts the hypothesis that institutional investors acquire flood-damaged properties at discounted prices. In this market, entity buyers (LLCs, corporations, trusts) *reduced* their flood zone exposure following the event.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Interpreting the "Freeze and Rebuild" Pattern

The results reveal a pattern of market adjustment that I characterize as "Freeze and Rebuild." At the SFHA boundary, transaction volume contracts sharply inside the flood zone---the "Freeze" component---while at the inundation boundary, the composition of transacting properties shifts toward newer and larger structures---the "Rebuild" component. Price effects are negative but imprecisely estimated, consistent with standard risk capitalization though not statistically distinguishable from zero. The composition shift suggests that market re-entry is selective: properties that transact post-flood inside the boundary are of systematically higher quality than pre-flood transactions.

Several mechanisms could generate the composition shift. First, insurance-funded repairs and rebuilding may upgrade the housing stock, with improved properties subsequently reaching market. The 818 NFIP claims totaling \$37.5 million provide the financial resources for substantial reconstruction. Second, owners of more damaged properties may defer sales while repairs are completed, generating a selection effect whereby only less-damaged (or fully rebuilt) properties transact in the post-period. Third, speculative developers may acquire damaged lots and construct new buildings, though the decline in entity purchases argues against large-scale investor acquisition.

Regardless of the precise mechanism, the composition shift has important implications for interpreting post-disaster price data. Studies that estimate price effects without accounting for selection may confound composition changes with treatment effects on valuations.

## Robustness and Identification Concerns

Several identification concerns merit discussion. First, the SFHA boundary fails the parallel trends test while the inundation boundary passes. This pattern may reflect systematic pre-trend differences in SFHA areas (older housing stock, different neighborhood trajectories) that are less pronounced at the inundation edge. I emphasize results at the inundation boundary for price effects. Importantly, the two boundaries show different sale rate dynamics: the SFHA boundary exhibits significant liquidity decline (the "Freeze"), while the inundation boundary shows increased sale rates inside, potentially reflecting rebuilt properties returning to market.

Second, the McCrary density tests show significant discontinuities at both boundaries. However, these reflect historical development patterns---higher parcel density outside the SFHA has persisted for decades---rather than post-flood manipulation of boundary assignment.

Third, the composition decomposition relies on observable characteristics and cannot account for unobservable quality changes. If post-flood sales are positively selected on unobservables (e.g., less flood damage, better condition), the decomposition will understate the true composition effect. Selection correction methods (Heckman, Lee bounds) yield similar qualitative conclusions but are imprecisely estimated given sample sizes.

## Policy Implications

The findings suggest several policy implications. First, post-disaster price monitoring should account for composition effects. Rising prices in flood zones need not indicate underpricing of risk if the transacting stock has shifted toward newer or improved structures. Second, transaction volume may be a more reliable early indicator of market distress than prices, as liquidity effects appear more quickly and precisely than price adjustments. Third, disclosure and mitigation policies should extend beyond regulatory boundaries to the "near-but-dry" ring where demand substitution concentrates.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This paper documents a "Freeze and Rebuild" pattern of housing market adjustment following the March 2019 Missouri River flood. At the SFHA boundary, transaction volume contracts sharply inside, with sale rates declining approximately 38 percent. Price effects are negative but imprecisely estimated (DiD = -0.26; 95% CI: [-0.85, +0.33]), consistent with standard flood risk capitalization though small sample sizes limit statistical precision. Crucially, the composition of transacting properties shifts systematically: post-flood sales are skewed toward newer and larger structures, consistent with rebuilding activity or selective market re-entry. Entity buyer share decreases substantially, contradicting investor acquisition hypotheses.

These findings have methodological implications for the large literature on flood risk capitalization. Post-disaster price effects may conflate treatment with selection if the composition of transacting properties shifts. They also have policy implications: monitoring transaction volume and property characteristics---not just prices---is essential for understanding post-disaster market dynamics. The "Freeze and Rebuild" pattern documented here may generalize to other disaster settings where insurance and rebuilding reshape the housing stock, though replication across contexts with different institutions and housing markets is warranted.
